question: What is the general New Jersey requirement for personal flotation devices (PFDs) aboard a recreational vessel underway?
choice_a: PFDs are optional for adults on any New Jersey waterway
choice_b: There must be one U.S. Coast Guard-approved, wearable PFD of the proper size for each person on board, readily accessible
choice_c: Only the operator is required to have a PFD available
choice_d: PFDs are only required on vessels longer than 40 feet
explanation: New Jersey, consistent with federal requirements, mandates one properly fitted, USCG-approved wearable PFD for every person aboard, and it must be readily accessible, not locked away or buried under gear.
source_note: NJSP Marine Services Bureau equipment checklist; federal USCG PFD carriage requirements

question: Under New Jersey's cold-weather PFD rule, when must PFDs be actually worn (not just carried) aboard vessels under 26 feet while underway?
choice_b: New Jersey has no seasonal wear requirement
choice_d: Only during the month of January
explanation: New Jersey requires all persons aboard recreational vessels under 26 feet to actually wear a USCG-approved PFD, not merely have one stowed aboard, while underway between November 1 and May 1, when cold-water immersion risk is highest.
source_note: NJSP Marine Services Bureau FAQ; N.J.A.C. 13:82 seasonal PFD-wear requirement

question: What is a Type III PFD most commonly used for?
choice_a: Offshore emergency use in remote or rough water where rescue may be delayed
choice_b: A throwable device tossed to a person in the water
choice_c: Only for use by children under age five
choice_d: General boating and water sports flotation aid, worn continuously, though it may not turn an unconscious wearer face-up
explanation: A Type III flotation aid is designed for general recreational boating and water sports where help is nearby, and it is the most commonly worn PFD type, though it is not designed to turn an unconscious person face-up like a Type I.
source_note: USCG PFD classification system, taught in NJ-approved NASBLA boater education courses

question: Which PFD type provides the greatest flotation and is designed to turn most unconscious wearers face-up in the water, making it best suited for offshore or rough water use?
choice_d: Type V (used only as a seat cushion)
explanation: A Type I offshore life jacket provides the most buoyancy of the wearable types and is specifically designed to turn an unconscious wearer face-up, making it ideal for open, rough, or remote water where rescue could take time.

question: What is a Type IV PFD, and what is a key limitation on how it may be used?
choice_a: A device used exclusively on personal watercraft
choice_b: A throwable device, such as a ring buoy or buoyant cushion, that must never be used as a substitute for a wearable PFD
choice_c: A wearable vest intended for infants only
choice_d: An inflatable belt pack that automatically counts toward the per-person wearable PFD requirement even when not worn
explanation: A Type IV device is a throwable flotation aid, like a boat cushion or ring buoy, meant to be thrown to a person in the water and grasped -- it does not satisfy the per-person wearable PFD requirement.

question: Under New Jersey law, is a stand-up paddleboard (SUP) user ever exempt from PFD requirements?
choice_a: SUPs are banned outright on all New Jersey waters
choice_b: SUP users are exempt only if they are certified lifeguards
choice_c: Yes -- a SUP used within the narrow limits of a designated swimming, surfing, or bathing area is exempt from the PFD requirement that otherwise applies
choice_d: No, SUP users must always wear a Type I offshore PFD regardless of location
explanation: New Jersey exempts stand-up paddleboards from PFD carriage/wear rules only when used within the limited confines of a designated swimming, surfing, or bathing area; outside those areas, a SUP is treated as a vessel and PFD rules apply.
source_note: NJSP Marine Services Bureau FAQ, SUP/paddleboard PFD exemption

question: For vessels 16 feet and longer (excluding canoes and kayaks), what additional PFD is generally required beyond one wearable PFD per person?
choice_a: A second full set of wearable PFDs for every passenger
choice_b: A life raft rated for ocean use
choice_c: No additional device is required beyond the wearable PFDs
choice_d: At least one Type IV throwable flotation device that is immediately accessible
explanation: Federal and New Jersey equipment rules require vessels 16 feet or longer, other than canoes and kayaks, to carry at least one throwable Type IV device in addition to a wearable PFD for each person aboard.
source_note: Federal USCG PFD carriage requirements applied in New Jersey

question: What should a boater check regularly to make sure a PFD will actually perform in an emergency?
choice_a: That it is the correct size for the wearer, in serviceable condition with no rips or waterlogged flotation material, and USCG-approved
choice_b: That it matches the color of the boat
choice_c: That it has never been worn before
choice_d: PFD condition does not need to be checked once purchased
explanation: A PFD must be properly sized, undamaged, and USCG-approved to function correctly; waterlogged foam, rips, or an oversized/undersized fit can all reduce a PFD's ability to keep a person afloat.
source_note: Universal PFD maintenance guidance in NASBLA-aligned boating courses

question: Why is an inflatable Type V PFD only counted toward the legal PFD requirement under certain conditions?
choice_a: Inflatable PFDs are always exempt from any restriction
choice_b: Because it must be worn, not simply stowed, to be legally credited as meeting the wearable PFD requirement
choice_c: Because inflatable PFDs are illegal in New Jersey
choice_d: Because Type V PFDs only work for children
explanation: A Type V special-use PFD, including many inflatable models, is only approved for use under specific conditions -- typically it must actually be worn as prescribed on its label to count toward the legal PFD requirement.
source_note: USCG PFD classification system, Type V special-use conditions

question: Under federal law that New Jersey enforces on its waters, what PFD-wear rule applies specifically to children?
choice_a: Only children under age 2 must wear a PFD
choice_b: Children may substitute a pool noodle for a PFD
choice_c: Children under 13 must wear a USCG-approved PFD while underway on the open deck of a vessel, unless below deck or in an enclosed cabin
choice_d: Children are exempt from all PFD requirements
explanation: Federal law requires children under 13 to wear a USCG-approved PFD whenever a recreational vessel is underway on the open deck, unless the child is below deck or within an enclosed cabin, and New Jersey enforces this rule on its waters.
source_note: Federal child PFD-wear requirement (33 CFR 175.15) enforced statewide including New Jersey
